
stem: Put these narrowing features in the order they arrived in TypeScript, from oldest to newest.

options.text: Narrowing through aliased conditions (`const isStr = typeof x === "string"`)
options.why: TypeScript 4.4.

options.text: Narrowing destructured discriminated unions
options.why: TypeScript 4.6.

options.text: `in` narrowing of keys an object does not list, such as on `object`
options.why: TypeScript 4.9.

options.text: `switch (true)` narrowing
options.why: TypeScript 5.3.

options.text: Inferred type predicates, such as in `.filter(x => x !== undefined)`
options.why: TypeScript 5.5.

explanation: Narrowing has improved steadily: aliased conditions in 4.4, destructured discriminants in 4.6, unlisted-key `in` narrowing in 4.9, `switch (true)` in 5.3, closure preservation in 5.4 and inferred predicates in 5.5. Knowing the versions explains why older codebases are full of workarounds that now look unnecessary.

stem: Which statements about assertion functions are true under TypeScript 6? (Choose three.)

options.text: An assertion function must return `void`; `return true` in a body declared `asserts v is string` is a type error
options.why: TS2322: type boolean is not assignable to type void.

options.text: Narrowing only applies when the assertion is called as a statement on its own, not when its result is assigned
options.why: `const r = assertDefined(x)` does not narrow `x`.

options.text: A `const` arrow can be an assertion function if the variable has an explicit function type annotation
options.why: The explicit annotation satisfies the TS2775 requirement.

options.text: An `async` function can be declared to return `Promise<asserts x is T>`
options.why: Rejected with TS1228: an assertion can only be the return type itself, so it can't be wrapped in a Promise.

options.text: Assertion functions are checked by the compiler to throw whenever the asserted type is wrong
options.why: Like type predicates, the body is trusted, not verified.

explanation: Assertion functions (TypeScript 3.7) narrow the rest of the scope after a call statement, because a failed check throws. They must be synchronous, return `void`, and be called through names with explicit types. Their bodies are trusted, so an assertion that forgets to throw is as dangerous as a wrong type predicate.
